扉.meaning: A fishmonger nails a big <part>fishbone</part> across her shop's <part>door</part> as a knocker. Visitors tap it and the bones ring out like a xylophone. It's the fanciest <kanji>front door</kanji> on the street.
扉.on: One lady knocks with the <sound>hee</sound>l of her shoe instead.
扉.kun: A cat on <sound>to</sound>p of the door eyes the fishbone, while a <sound>bee</sound> eyes the cat's bowl of <sound>ra</sound>men.

隆.meaning: A gardener plants a seedling bursting with <part>life</part> in a flat field, sets a <part>folding chair</part> beside it and plants a little <part>pennant</part> to mark the spot. Every day the ground under the chair swells higher, until the roots have pushed up a giant <kanji>hump</kanji>.
隆.on: Years later the gardener's whole family holds a <sound>reu</sound>nion on top of it.

后.meaning: Standing on a <part>cliff</part> top, a lady in a crown snaps her fan shut and opens her <part>mouth</part>: the whole army below falls silent. The king hides behind her cape. Everyone knows who really rules: the <kanji>empress</kanji>.
后.on: Then she hands every soldier an ice cream <sound>co</sound>ne.
后.kun: Her pet <sound>ki</sound>wi bird dips its cone in <sound>sa</sound>lsa, then hands her the <sound>key</sound>s to the palace.

帥.meaning: In the duck pond army, an old drake ties a <part>towel</part> to a <part>pole</part> and waves it, quacking orders from a wide-open <part>mouth</part>. Two hundred ducklings swim in perfect rows behind him. He is the <kanji>commander</kanji>.
帥.on: He pays each duckling with one wrapped <sound>swee</sound>t.

雰.meaning: A theatre makes soft, misty <part>rain</part> fall indoors over the stage, but only for one <part>part</part> of the play: the farewell scene. The lights dim and the audience sniffles. Nobody remembers the words afterwards, only the <kanji>atmosphere</kanji>.
雰.on: On opening night the rain machine jams and blows a full ty<sound>phoon</sound> into the front row.

剖.meaning: Twins argue over the last pie, so their granny climbs onto a <part>soapbox</part> in the kitchen, raises a butter knife like a <part>dagger</part> and gives a speech about fairness. Then, with one neat cut, she makes two exact halves. That's how you <kanji>divide</kanji>.
剖.on: The pie is as heavy as a <sound>bo</sound>ulder: each half still needs two hands.

猶.meaning: A magician pulls a <part>fishhook</part> from his hat. Then a rubber duck. Then a stick of <part>lit dynamite</part> that fizzes out into confetti. 'And <kanji>furthermore</kanji>…' he says, reaching in again, as the audience edges toward the door.
猶.on: The next thing out of the hat is a small, grumpy <sound>u</sound>nicorn.
猶.kun: It munches the front row's <sound>na</sound>chos, and the crowd gasps: '<sound>Oh</sound>!'

稽.meaning: A baker with a <part>broken crutch</part> hobbles to the mill every morning for <part>grain</part> and bakes the same loaf again and again. Burnt, flat, burnt, flat, until loaf three hundred comes out <part>delicious</part>. Nothing beats <kanji>practice</kanji>.
稽.on: To celebrate, loaf three hundred and one is a birthday <sound>ca</sound>ke.
稽.kun: He tucks a pink <sound>carn</sound>ation behind his ear and sniffs a bulb of <sound>ga</sound>rlic, dreaming up the next recipe.
